t: What mid, senior and lead actually mean
one: Levels differ less in what you know than in the size and ambiguity of problems you can own, and how much you multiply others.
an: Mid: given a well-drawn map, reaches the destination. Senior: draws the map for a region. Lead: decides which regions the team explores and gets everyone there.
how: Strong mid: delivers well-defined features end to end with little help; writes tested, readable code; knows when to ask.
Senior: turns vague problems into designs and shipped systems; owns production behaviour; makes trade-offs explicit; reviews and mentors; spots risks early.
Tech lead: sets technical direction for a team; breaks down projects; aligns with product and stakeholders; grows people; accountable for delivery and quality.
Interviews test level through system design depth, ambiguity handling and the scope of your past-project stories, not trivia.
why: Knowing the target lets you aim your learning and present your experience at the right level.
trade: Titles vary wildly across companies. A "senior" at a startup may be mid elsewhere and vice versa; read ladders, not titles.

myth.r: Years correlate loosely. Scope of ownership and judgement are what get you leveled.

q.s: Which story best signals senior level in an interview?
o: "I implemented the tickets assigned to me quickly."
"Our checkout had 2% failures; I found the cause, proposed a design with trade-offs, led the rollout and cut failures to 0.1%."
"I know 12 frameworks."
"I never had a bug."
q.e: Ambiguous problem → owned diagnosis, design, delivery and measured outcome.

more: Regional differences (e.g. Korean companies' 직급 vs Western levels)
lab: Read two public ladders. For each expectation at the next level, write one example from your work or mark it as a gap. Pick two gaps to close in the next 3 months.
Start a brag document: every shipped thing, its impact, and what you learned.
docs: Julia Evans: Get your work recognized: write a brag document

plain: Engineering levels mostly differ in the size and vagueness of problems you can handle alone, and how much you make others better. Strong mid: delivers clear features well. Senior: turns unclear problems into working systems and makes good trade-offs. Lead: sets direction for a team and delivers through others.
bridge: You are moving from “I build what is specified, well” to “I figure out what should be built, and make sure it works in production”.

walk.title: How the same project looks at each level
steps: Project: “Customers complain checkout is unreliable.”
Strong mid: given a specific bug ticket, fixes it cleanly with a test.
Senior: investigates the whole problem, finds three causes (timeouts, duplicate webhooks, a race condition), proposes a design, leads the fix, shows failures dropping from 2% to 0.1%.
Lead: decides this is the team's top priority this quarter, splits work among three people, aligns with product and support, and sets up monitoring so it stays fixed.
In interviews, you show your level through stories like these, not by listing technologies.

terms: A company's defined stages of engineering seniority.
How big and ambiguous your problems are.
The measurable result of your work.
insights: Leveling is decided from written interview notes. A number or a named decision is easy for the interviewer to write down; “I am a strong engineer” is not.
Collect evidence continuously (a “brag document”); you will need it for promotions and interviews, and you cannot rebuild it from memory.
Read the duties in a job posting, not only the title and the years; the duties show the real scope the team expects.

prod.summary: In real hiring, your level is decided by a committee or hiring manager reading interview notes against a written ladder. Coding rounds mostly decide pass or fail; system design depth and the scope of your project stories decide which level you are offered. A “down-level” (an offer one level below what you applied for) is a common, quiet outcome.
checklist: Read the company's public ladder (or levels.fyi) and map the role title to its real expectations before you apply.
For each target-level expectation (owns ambiguous problems, makes trade-offs, mentors), have one concrete story ready.
Keep a brag document updated monthly: what shipped, the metric it moved, who it helped. You cannot rebuild this from memory later.
In a Korean job posting, read both the years filter (e.g. “경력 3년 이상”) and the duties list; the duties tell you the real scope.
When comparing offers, compare scope, team size, on-call and growth path, not only title. “Senior” at a 10-person startup is often mid at a large company.
After a down-level offer, ask the recruiter which signals were missing; it is the most useful feedback you will get.
numbers: Dropbox's public career framework has 7 engineering IC levels (IC1–IC7); “Staff” starts at IC5.
Amazon's leadership principles, used to evaluate every level, number 16 (two were added in 2021: “Strive to be Earth's Best Employer” and “Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility”).
failures: You pass every coding round but get an offer one level lower than the role you applied for.
Your design round stayed at “boxes and arrows” and your stories were about finished tickets. Prepare one deep-dive on a hard decision you owned, with alternatives and a metric.
You have “Senior Engineer” on your CV but interviewers keep asking basic ownership questions.
Titles do not transfer between companies. Describe scope instead: “I designed and ran the payment retry system used by 40k users”, not “I was senior”.
Promotion review says “not enough evidence of impact” even though you worked hard.
Work was not written down or not linked to outcomes. Keep a brag document with links (PRs, dashboards, design docs) and the business result of each item.
A Korean posting asks for 5 years; you have 3 strong years and do not apply.
Years are often a soft filter. If your stories match the listed duties, apply and lead with scope; the worst case is a no or a lower level.

code.title: A brag-document entry that maps to a ladder
code.src:
Month: 2026-05
What: Fixed checkout failures (2% -> 0.1%)
My part: found 3 causes from logs (timeouts, duplicate
  webhooks, a race in order status); wrote the design doc;
  led rollout behind a flag; added an alert on failure rate
Scope: ambiguous problem, no ticket existed (senior signal)
Leverage: reviewed 2 teammates' PRs on idempotency keys;
  wrote the runbook support now uses
Evidence: PR #412, #418; dashboard link; design doc link
Ladder line: “Turns unclear problems into shipped systems”
code.note: The “Ladder line” is what makes this useful: each entry is evidence for one written expectation at the next level.

qs.s: You get two offers: “Senior Frontend Engineer” at a 12-person startup and “Software Engineer II” at a large company. How should you compare the level fairly?
o: Compare the actual scope: what you will own, how ambiguous the work is, who you learn from, and how each maps to a public ladder
Take the senior title, because titles move with you to the next job
Take the bigger company, because big-company levels are always higher
Compare only salary, because levels are marketing
qs.e: Titles do not transfer; scope and the ladder expectations do. The startup title can be fine, but the next interviewer will level you on what you owned, not on the word “senior”.

qs.s: Which brag-document entry is the strongest evidence for a promotion to senior?
o: “Closed 47 Jira tickets this quarter.”
“Learned Rust and Kubernetes.”
“Search was slow and nobody owned it. I measured it, found a missing index and an N+1 query, fixed both, and p95 latency fell from 1.4s to 120ms. Wrote a guide the team now uses.”
“Worked late every week to meet the deadline.”
qs.e: It shows an unowned, ambiguous problem, a diagnosis, a measured result and leverage (the guide). Ticket counts and hours worked show effort, not level.

qs.s: After an onsite loop you hear: “Strong coding, but design and project discussion were at mid level.” What is the most likely outcome?
o: Automatic rejection
An offer at a lower level than the role you applied for
A senior offer, because coding is the main signal
Another coding round
qs.e: Many companies down-level instead of rejecting. Coding is often the pass/fail gate; design and story scope decide the level.

qs.s: Read this hiring-committee summary for a candidate who applied for a senior role. What is the most likely outcome?

code.title: hiring-committee-notes.txt
code.src:
Coding (2 rounds):   strong hire, clean code, tested edge cases
System design:       lean hire. Drove requirements, sized the
                     DB with numbers. Discussed failure modes
                     only when prompted.
Project deep dive:   lean no-hire for senior. Story was a feature
                     inside a project the tech lead had designed;
                     could not explain why the queue was chosen.
Behavioral:          hire. Clear ownership of own tasks,
                     no example of influencing other teams.

o: A senior offer, because both coding rounds were strong hire
An offer one level down (mid), because design and project scope show mid-level ownership
A rejection, because one round was no-hire
A staff-level offer, because the coding was excellent
qs.e: Coding usually decides pass or fail; scope signals decide the level. Here the strongest negative is about ownership of decisions, which is exactly the senior bar, so a down-level is the common result. One lean no-hire on the level question is not the same as a no-hire on the candidate.

qs.s: Your performance review says the text below. Which change would most clearly move you toward senior?

code.title: review-2026-h1.txt
code.src:
Strengths:
  - Delivers assigned features on time, few bugs
  - Good PR descriptions, responsive in review
Growth areas:
  - Waits for the tech lead to write designs
  - Rarely raises risks during planning;
    problems appear late in the sprint
  - Impact is mostly inside own tickets

o: Deliver tickets faster and take more of them each sprint
Learn a second backend language to widen your skills
Volunteer to write the design doc for the next vague project, list its risks in planning, and track one metric after launch
Work extra hours so problems do not appear late in the sprint
qs.e: Every growth area is about ambiguity and ownership, not speed. Writing the design and naming risks early is the senior behaviour the review asks for. More tickets or more hours improves the strengths the reviewer already gave you.

qs.s: You are a strong senior who enjoys deep technical work. Your manager offers you a team-lead role with 5 direct reports. What is the most important trade-off to understand before you say yes?
o: A lead role always pays more, so there is no real trade-off

Your impact moves from your own code to people and planning work (1:1s, hiring, alignment); many companies also have a staff-engineer IC track that grows scope without reports, so ask whether it exists here
You will keep coding the same amount, plus a few meetings
Once you take a lead role you can never return to IC work
qs.e: The change is in how you create impact, not just in title. Many companies run parallel IC and manager ladders (Dropbox's public framework has IC levels up to IC7). Moving back to IC is common, so “never return” is false, and keeping full coding time with 5 reports is rarely realistic.

qs.s: You have 4 years at a 15-person startup where your title is “Senior Engineer”. A large company's recruiter asks what level you are targeting. Best answer?
o: “Senior, because that is my current title.”
“Whatever you think; I'm happy with any level.”
“Staff, so I have room to negotiate down.”
Describe your scope (what you owned end to end, how ambiguous it was, who you led), say you are aiming for senior, and ask how their loop decides the level
qs.e: Titles do not transfer, but scope does, and recruiters use it to pick the right loop. Anchoring on the title alone sounds naive; aiming far above your evidence usually leads to a no-hire instead of a down-level.

interview.q: In your view, what does a senior engineer do that a mid-level engineer does not?
answer: Takes a vague problem (“checkout is unreliable”) and turns it into a scoped plan and design, instead of waiting for tickets.
Owns production behaviour: metrics, alerts, rollout plan and rollback, not only the merged PR.
Makes trade-offs explicit in writing (“X costs Y, acceptable because Z”) and changes their mind when data says so.
Raises risks early in planning and pushes back on scope with reasons.
Multiplies others: reviews that teach, docs and runbooks, unblocking teammates.
Backs every point with one short real example from your own work; a list of traits alone scores low.
followups: Give me an example of when you did that.
What is the gap between you and the next level right now?

interview.q: Tell me about the most ambiguous problem you owned from start to finish.
answer: Starts from a problem without a clear solution or owner, not a well-defined ticket.
Shows how you reduced ambiguity: data you gathered, people you talked to, the options you considered.
Names the decision and its cost, and who you had to convince.
Covers delivery: how you split the work, rolled it out safely, and measured the result.
Ends with a number and what you would do differently.
followups: What did you decide not to do?
Who disagreed, and how did you handle it?
How did you know it worked?

interview.q: How do you make the engineers around you more effective?
answer: Concrete mechanisms, not attitude: a code-review habit, a design-doc template, a runbook, pairing sessions.
One example with evidence: “after my guide on idempotency keys, two teammates shipped retries without help”.
Shows you adjust to the person: more context for a new joiner, more autonomy for a strong peer.
Mentions removing friction for the team (flaky tests, slow CI, unclear ownership).
Admits a limit: what did not work and what you changed.
followups: Tell me about someone you mentored. How did they grow?
How do you give hard feedback in code review?

videos.t: What does "Senior" Software Engineer mean? (From a Senior Software Engineer)

one: Timed algorithm problems still gate many companies, including most large Korean employers' 코딩테스트. They are learnable by pattern, not by memorising problems.
an: Learning chess openings and tactics, not specific games: you recognise the shape of the position and know the moves that fit.
how: Core patterns: hash maps, two pointers, sliding window, binary search, BFS/DFS, heaps, intervals, prefix sums, dynamic programming basics, union-find, topological sort. Korean coding tests also lean heavily on 구현 (careful simulation of long specs).
Know Big-O for your solution and the standard data structures in your interview language.
Process in live interviews: restate, ask about edge cases, propose brute force, improve, code cleanly, test with examples out loud.
Practise on timed sets: LeetCode, 프로그래머스, 백준. Review failures by pattern.
why: Strong engineers fail these through lack of practice, not ability. A few months of steady pattern practice changes outcomes.
trade: Grinding hundreds of problems without reviewing patterns gives poor returns. Mix with system design and project prep for senior roles.

myth.r: Many companies still screen with them at every level. Seniors are just expected to also do design.

q.s: Given an array and k, find the longest subarray with at most k distinct values. Which pattern fits?
o: Binary search on the answer
Sliding window with a hash map of counts
Topological sort
Union-find
q.e: Expand the right edge, shrink the left while distinct count > k.

more: Korean coding test formats (프로그래머스 level system, 구현/시뮬레이션)
lab: Do 3 problems a week from one pattern at a time, timed. After each, write the pattern name and the key insight in one line.
Do one full timed 프로그래머스 or company-style test per month and review every miss.

plain:
Coding interviews give you an algorithm problem with a time limit. They are learnable: most problems use one of about 15 patterns (hash maps, two pointers, sliding window, binary search, BFS/DFS, heaps, dynamic programming...). Learn to recognise the pattern, and the problem becomes much easier.

Korean company coding tests also include long “implementation” problems where you must carefully simulate a detailed specification.
bridge: You already use some of these daily: a Map for fast lookups is the hash map pattern, and a rate limiter that counts requests in the last 60 seconds is a sliding window. Interviews just ask you to use them under time pressure.

walk.title: Solving a problem out loud
steps: Problem: find the longest substring without repeating characters.
Restate and check examples: “abcabcbb” → “abc”, length 3. Ask about empty strings and character set.
Brute force first: check every substring, O(n²) or worse. Say it, then improve.
Recognise the pattern: sliding window with a set (or map of last positions). Move the right edge; when a repeat appears, move the left edge past it. O(n).
Code it cleanly, then walk through “abba” by hand to test edge cases.

terms: How time or memory grows with input size.
A reusable approach like sliding window or BFS.
Korean coding-test category: careful simulation of detailed rules.
insights: After every practice problem, write the pattern name and the key insight in one line. Reviewing that list beats solving new problems blindly.
The constraint line is a hint. Very small n (about 20) often allows brute force or backtracking; n ≤ 10^5 needs about O(n log n); huge n (10^9) points to O(log n) or math.
A live round is graded on the process you show, not only on the final code.

prod.summary: In Korea, large employers run online coding tests on platforms such as 프로그래머스 (Programmers): you complete a solution() function and hidden test cases grade both correctness (정확성) and speed (효율성). Samsung runs its own offline test with standard input/output. International companies mostly use live 45–60 minute rounds where talking through your approach counts as much as the code. Seniors are still screened this way.
checklist: Read the constraints first and pick the target complexity: n ≤ 10^5 means you need about O(n log n) or better.
Know your test platform's format: Programmers = fill in solution() and return a value; 백준 and Samsung = read stdin, print stdout. Practise in that exact format.
Know your language's standard tools cold: Map/Set, sorting with a comparator, a queue for BFS, and that JavaScript has no built-in heap.
In live rounds: restate, ask about edge cases, state brute force and its Big-O, then improve before coding.
Test out loud with an empty input, a single element, duplicates and the largest input size.
For long Korean 구현 problems, write the rules as a short list before coding; most bugs are a misread rule, not a wrong algorithm.
In timed tests, budget time per problem and move on when stuck; problems are often ordered easy to hard.
numbers: Kakao's 2023 blind recruitment first-round online coding test had 7 problems over 5 hours (tech.kakao.com).
Programmers PCCP certification: 4 coding problems in 120 minutes, one language from Python, JavaScript, Java, C, C++ or C#, webcam-proctored, valid for 2 years.

Samsung's SW 역량테스트 is taken on test-centre PCs (no internet); recent reports describe 2 problems in about 4 hours in C, C++, Java or Python. Check the current notice, the format has changed over the years.
Rule of thumb: about 10^8 simple operations per second in C++, far fewer in Python or JavaScript, so O(n²) with n = 10^5 (10^10 steps) will time out anywhere.
failures: Programmers shows all 정확성 cases passing but 효율성 cases fail with “시간 초과” (time limit exceeded).
Your algorithm is too slow for large inputs, often an Array.includes or indexOf inside a loop (hidden O(n²)). Replace it with a Set/Map lookup or a sliding window.
Your solution passes the examples but fails hidden tests with a wrong answer.
Edge cases: empty input, all equal values, very large numbers, or a window that moves backwards (the classic “abba” bug). Write those cases yourself before submitting.
In a live round you solve the problem silently and still get “no hire”.
The interviewer could not see your reasoning. Narrate: the brute force, why it is slow, the pattern you chose, and how you test it.
You spend 90 minutes of a 5-hour test on problem 4 and never read problems 5–7.
No time budget. Skim all problems first, solve the ones you can finish, and come back to the hard one.
A JavaScript solution gives wrong order after arr.sort() on numbers.
Default sort compares strings, so 10 comes before 9. Always pass a comparator: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b).

code.title: Sliding window: longest substring without repeating characters
code.note: The prev >= left check is the line interviewers look for: a character seen before the window started must not move the left edge backwards. On Programmers you would wrap this in function solution(s) and return the number.

qs.s: A Programmers problem says n ≤ 100,000. Your nested-loop solution passes every 정확성 test but fails 효율성. What does this tell you?
o: The platform is slow; resubmit in C++
You need to add caching to the inner loop
O(n²) is about 10^10 steps at this size; you need an O(n) or O(n log n) approach such as a hash map, sorting or a sliding window
You have an off-by-one error
qs.e: Correct output on small cases plus a timeout on big ones means the algorithm, not the language, is the problem. Switching to C++ does not save 10^10 operations.

qs.s: In the sliding-window code above, someone deletes && prev >= left. Which input now returns a wrong answer?
o: "abcabcbb"
"abba"
"bbbbb"
qs.e: At the last “a”, its old index 0 is before the window (left = 2). Without the check, left jumps back to 1 and the window “bba” of length 3 is counted. The other inputs never see a repeat outside the window.

qs.s: Kakao-style test: 5 hours, 7 problems. After 3 hours you solved 1–3 and have spent 70 minutes stuck on #4. Best move?
o: Skim #5–#7, solve the one with the clearest rules (often an implementation problem), then return to #4 with the time left
Keep going on #4; problems must be solved in order
Stop and review problems 1–3 for the rest of the time
Submit a partial #4 and end the test early
qs.e: Problems are not graded in order, and a later problem with clear rules may be faster than a stuck one. Time budgeting is part of the test.

qs.s: A candidate writes this two-sum solution (return indices of two different elements that add up to target). Which input returns a wrong answer?

code.title: twoSum.ts

o: [2, 7, 11, 15], target 9
[1, 5, 9], target 14
[-1, 4, 0], target 3
[3, 2, 4], target 6
qs.e: The value is stored before the lookup, so at i = 0 the element 3 finds itself (6 − 3 = 3) and returns [0, 0]. Fix: look up first, then set. The other inputs only find a partner that was stored earlier, so they return correct pairs and hide the bug.

qs.s: This binary search should return the largest x in [0, n] where ok(x) is true (ok is true up to some point, then false). On some inputs it never returns. Why?

code.title: lastTrue.ts

o: lo + hi overflows for large n
When hi = lo + 1 and ok(lo) is true, mid rounds down to lo, so lo = mid makes no progress; round up instead: Math.floor((lo + hi + 1) / 2)
The loop condition must be lo <= hi
ok must be called twice per step
qs.e: With lo = 3, hi = 4: mid = 3, ok(3) is true, lo stays 3, forever. When the “true” branch keeps mid, mid must round up. Overflow is a real issue for 32-bit ints in Java or C++, but JavaScript numbers are exact up to 2^53, and it would give a wrong answer, not a hang.

qs.s: A problem says n ≤ 2,000. You have a correct O(n²) dynamic-programming solution with 25 minutes left in a live round. What should you do?
o: Keep it: 2,000² = 4 million steps runs well inside any time limit; use the time to test edge cases and explain complexity
Rewrite it in O(n log n) before testing, because interviewers always want the optimal bound
Switch to a recursive version without memoisation, because it is shorter
Ask for a bigger time limit
qs.e: Constraints tell you the target. 4 × 10^6 simple steps is fast even in JavaScript or Python. Spending the last 25 minutes on an unneeded rewrite risks ending with broken code and no testing, which costs more than a non-optimal bound.

qs.s: Read this part of a live-interview transcript. What is the biggest gap the interviewer will write down?

code.title: transcript.txt
code.src:
[05:10] Candidate: So I restate: merge all overlapping
        intervals. Brute force compares every pair, O(n^2).
[07:30] Candidate: If I sort by start, I only need to
        compare with the last merged interval. O(n log n).
[08:00] (types code for 14 minutes, silent)
[22:10] Candidate: Done. I think it works.
[22:15] Interviewer: Can you try [[1,4],[4,5]]?
[23:40] Candidate: Oh, I used < instead of <=, so it
        doesn't merge them. Let me fix that.

o: The candidate should have started with the optimal solution
Sorting was the wrong idea; a heap is needed
Restating the problem wasted time
They stopped talking while coding and did not test their own code; the interviewer had to find the edge case
qs.e: The approach and complexity were strong. The weak signal is verification: no tracing of examples, no touching-interval case, and 14 silent minutes. Brute force first is the recommended process, not a mistake.

interview.q: Coding problem: given a list of intervals like [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10]], merge all overlapping intervals.
answer: Clarify first: is the input sorted? Do touching intervals like [1,4] and [4,5] merge? Can the input be empty?
Key approach: sort by start (O(n log n)), then scan once; if the next start ≤ the last merged end, extend the end with max; otherwise push a new interval.
The max matters: [1,10] then [2,3] must stay [1,10], not shrink to [1,3].
Complexity: O(n log n) time for the sort, O(n) extra space for the output.
Test out loud: empty list, one interval, nested interval, touching intervals, unsorted input.
followups: Insert one new interval into an already sorted, merged list in O(n).
What changes if intervals arrive one by one as a stream?

interview.q: Coding problem: a grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water) is given. Count the islands (groups of land connected up, down, left, right).
answer: Key approach: scan every cell; when you find unvisited land, increase the count and flood-fill the whole island with BFS or DFS, marking cells as visited.
Complexity: O(rows × cols) time, because each cell is visited a constant number of times.
Production-minded detail: recursive DFS on a 1000 × 1000 all-land grid can overflow the call stack in JavaScript; use an explicit stack or queue.
Say whether you mutate the input to mark visited (cheaper) or keep a separate visited array (safer if the caller reuses the grid).
Alternative: union-find, which also works when land is added over time.
followups: Return the size of the largest island.
Land cells are added one at a time; report the island count after each addition.

interview.q: Coding problem: given an array of numbers and k, return the k most frequent elements.
answer: Key approach: count with a hash map in O(n).
Then either sort the entries by count (O(m log m) for m distinct values), keep a min-heap of size k (O(m log k)), or bucket by count (O(n)).
Mention the language detail: JavaScript has no built-in heap, so bucket sort or a sort is the practical choice in a 45-minute round.
Clarify ties and output order with the interviewer before coding.
Test: k equal to the number of distinct values, all elements equal, negative numbers.
followups: The data is a stream that does not fit in memory. What changes?
Why might a heap be better than bucket sort for very large n and small k?

videos.t: How to Solve ANY Coding Interview Question in 6 Steps
videos.why: A six-step method for any coding question.
What coding interviews look like now.

one: A 45–60 minute conversation where you design a system (a URL shortener, a chat app, a feed) and are judged on structure, trade-offs and depth, not one right answer.
an: Sketching a house with a client: you ask how many people will live there before deciding on bedrooms, and explain why the kitchen goes where it does.
how: A reliable flow: requirements (functional + non-functional: scale, latency, consistency) → estimates → API → data model → high-level design → deep dives on the hardest parts → bottlenecks and failure modes.
Drive the conversation, state assumptions, and name trade-offs explicitly ("I'll use eventual consistency for like counts because...").
Everything in this atlas's system design, database, caching and messaging tracks is the raw material.
Frontend-heavy candidates may get frontend system design: component architecture, data fetching, caching, performance, accessibility for a product like a news feed or an autocomplete.
why: It is the main senior-level signal in interviews and mirrors the real job of designing systems with others.
trade: Over-engineering (Kafka, sharding, microservices for 10 requests per second) is a common failure. Size the design to the stated scale.

myth.m: There is one correct design I need to memorise.
myth.r: Interviewers grade reasoning, prioritisation and trade-offs. Different designs can all score well.

q.s: First 5 minutes of "Design a URL shortener". What should you do?
o: Start drawing Kafka and Cassandra
Clarify requirements and scale: reads vs writes per second, custom aliases, expiry, analytics, latency targets
Write code
Pick a database brand
q.e: Requirements and numbers decide every later choice.

more: Classic problems: URL shortener, rate limiter, news feed, chat, notification system, file storage, search autocomplete
lab: Do one design per week out loud with a 45-minute timer, recording yourself or with a friend. Use the flow above and write the final diagram.
After each, compare with a reference write-up and list what you missed.
docs: Hello Interview: System design in a hurry

plain: In a system design interview you design a system (a URL shortener, chat app, news feed) in 45–60 minutes. There is no single right answer. You are judged on how you clarify requirements, estimate scale, structure the design, and explain trade-offs.
bridge: You already do a small version of this at work: before building a feature you ask product what it must do and for how many users, sketch the API and data, and discuss the risky parts. The interview compresses that into 45 minutes and asks you to say every reason out loud.

walk.title: The first 15 minutes of “Design a URL shortener”
steps: Clarify: custom aliases? expiry? analytics? How many new links per day, how many clicks?
Estimate: 1M new links/day ≈ 12/s; 100M clicks/day ≈ 1,200/s, peak ~5,000/s. Reads dominate.
API: POST /links {url} → short code; GET /:code → 301/302 redirect.
Data: table links(code PK, url, created_at, owner). 1M/day × 500 bytes ≈ 180GB/year: one database is fine.
Design: generate codes (base62 of an ID), cache hot codes in Redis, CDN for redirects, async click analytics via a queue. Then deep-dive where the interviewer points.

terms: Detailed discussion of one hard part.
insights: Draw the simple version first. Adding a cache or queue later, with the problem it solves, scores better than starting with them.
Before the deep dive, ask where to go deeper; the answer tells you what the interviewer wants to grade.
For every box you draw, have an answer ready for “what happens when this goes down?”

prod.summary: Real system design rounds are 45–60 minutes with an interviewer who pushes on your weakest point. Strong candidates spend about the first 5 minutes on requirements, sketch a simple design that works, then go deep on one or two hard parts (data model, hot keys, failure modes). The grade is about judgement: does each component exist for a reason you can state?
checklist: Write functional and non-functional requirements on the board before any boxes: scale, latency target, consistency needs, read/write ratio.
Do math only when it changes a decision (one database or sharded? cache needed?), and round aggressively: 1 day ≈ 10^5 seconds.
Define the API and the data model, including the primary key and the main query; most later questions come back to these.
Start with the simplest design that meets the numbers, then add parts (cache, queue, replicas) and say what problem each one solves.
For every component, be ready for “what happens if this goes down?”: timeouts, retries, fallbacks, and what the user sees.
Name trade-offs as sentences: “I choose X; it costs Y; that is fine because Z.”
Frontend roles: expect component structure, data fetching and caching, race conditions, performance budgets and accessibility.
numbers: 1 million requests per day is about 12 per second on average (86,400 seconds in a day); peak is commonly assumed to be 2–5× the average.
Hello Interview's delivery framework suggests about 5 minutes on requirements, about 10–15 on the high-level design and about 10 on deep dives in a 45-minute round.
failures: You draw Kafka, Cassandra and microservices in the first 10 minutes; the interviewer asks “why?” and you cannot answer with a number.
Design before requirements. Restart from the stated scale; at a few hundred requests per second one Postgres plus a cache is usually enough.
The interviewer asks “what if the cache goes down?” and you say “it won't”.
No failure thinking. Describe the real effect: every request hits the database, possible overload; then the fix: request coalescing, rate limits, replicas, and a warm-up plan.
Time runs out while you are still listing requirements or doing long estimates.
No time-boxing. Keep requirements to about 5 minutes and do math only when it drives a choice.
You give a monologue and miss the hints the interviewer gives about where to go deep.
It is a conversation. Check in after the high-level design: “Which part would you like me to go deeper on?”

code.title: Back-of-envelope worksheet: URL shortener
code.src:
Assumptions (say them out loud)
  new links:   1M / day
  redirects:   100M / day   (read:write = 100:1)

Throughput   (1 day = 86,400 s; use ~10^5 s for quick math)
  writes   1M / 86,400     ~ 12 / s
  reads    100M / 86,400   ~ 1,200 / s, peak x3-5 ~ 3,500-6,000 / s

Storage
  1 row ~ 500 B -> 1M x 500 B = 500 MB / day ~ 180 GB / year

Decisions the numbers drive
  - 12 writes/s: one primary database is enough
  - ~6,000 reads/s at peak, heavy skew to popular links: cache hot codes
  - 180 GB/year: no sharding needed for years
  - short code: base62 of 7 chars = 62^7 ~ 3.5 trillion codes
code.note: Every number ends in a decision. A calculation that only proves “it is a lot” wastes interview time.

qs.s: An app has 50 million daily active users, and each reads the feed 20 times a day. Roughly how many feed reads per second should you plan for?
o: About 1,200 per second
About 116,000 per second on average
About 1 million per second
About 11,600 per second on average, with peaks perhaps 2–3× higher
qs.e: 50M × 20 = 10^9 reads per day; 10^9 / 86,400 ≈ 11,600 per second. Peaks are higher than the average, so you plan capacity for the peak.

qs.s: You put Redis in front of Postgres for hot URL codes. The interviewer asks: “Redis restarts at peak. What happens?” Best answer?
o: All reads fall through to Postgres at once; I would size or protect the database for that (request coalescing, rate limits, read replicas) and warm the cache for the top codes
Nothing, Redis is in memory so it is fast
Users see errors until Redis comes back, which is acceptable
I would add a second Kafka cluster
qs.e: The real risk is a thundering herd: a sudden flood of cache misses that can overload the database. Seniors name the failure and the protection, not just the happy path.

qs.s: Frontend system design: “Design a search autocomplete.” Which deep dive shows the most production judgement?
o: Choosing between CSS modules and Tailwind
Which state library to use

Debouncing input, cancelling stale requests (e.g. AbortController) so old responses cannot overwrite new ones, caching recent queries, and keyboard/screen-reader support with the ARIA combobox pattern
Adding a loading spinner
qs.e: Race conditions, request volume, caching and accessibility are the hard, real problems in autocomplete. Styling and library choice are minor details here.

qs.s: Read this candidate's rate-limiter design. The interviewer asks the question at the end. What is the correct answer?

code.title: whiteboard.txt
code.src:
Limit: 100 requests per minute per API key

key   = "rl:" + apiKey + ":" + currentMinute
count = INCR key          (Redis)
if count == 1: EXPIRE key 60
if count > 100: return 429

Interviewer: a client sends 100 requests at 12:00:59
and 100 more at 12:01:00. What happens?

o: The second batch is rejected, because the 12:00 key is still alive
Some requests are double counted, because INCR is not atomic
All 200 are accepted within about one second: a fixed window allows up to 2× the limit at a boundary; a sliding-window counter or a token bucket fixes this if strict limits matter
Redis returns an error because the key already has a TTL
qs.e: 12:01:00 uses a new key with count 0, so the fixed window resets exactly at the boundary. INCR itself is atomic in Redis, so double counting is not the issue. A strong candidate also says when the burst is acceptable (cheap endpoints) and when it is not (login, payments).

qs.s: Design a chat app: 10 million daily active users send 40 messages each per day; one stored message is about 200 bytes. How much message storage per day and per year?
o: About 8 GB per day, about 3 TB per year
About 80 GB per day, about 29 TB per year
About 800 GB per day, about 290 TB per year
About 80 TB per day
qs.e: 10^7 × 40 = 4 × 10^8 messages; × 200 B = 8 × 10^10 B = 80 GB per day; × 365 ≈ 29 TB per year (before replicas and indexes). That size pushes you to partition by conversation and time, and to move old messages to cheaper storage. The decision is the point of the math.

qs.s: News feed design. Most users have 200 followers, but a few celebrities have 50 million. You chose fan-out on write (copy each new post into every follower's feed). The interviewer asks about celebrities. Best answer?
o: Use a hybrid: fan-out on write for normal users, but fetch celebrity posts at read time and merge them into the feed
Keep fan-out on write and add more workers until it is fast enough
Switch everyone to fan-out on read, because write fan-out is always wrong
Limit celebrities to 1 million followers
qs.e: One celebrity post would mean 50 million feed writes, a huge spike of work and delay. Pulling those few accounts at read time removes the spike while keeping reads cheap for everyone else. Pure fan-out on read makes every feed load expensive, which is the wrong cost for a read-heavy product.

qs.s: A candidate generates random 7-character codes for a URL shortener and saves them like this (code is the primary key). Two servers pick the same code at the same moment. What happens, and what is the right fix?

code.title: create-link.sql
code.src:
-- app picks code = random base62, 7 chars
SELECT 1 FROM links WHERE code = $1;   -- returns no row
-- no row, so insert
INSERT INTO links (code, url) VALUES ($1, $2);

o: Both inserts succeed and one link silently points to the wrong URL
Wrap both statements in a SERIALIZABLE transaction; nothing else will work

Both SELECTs see no row; the second INSERT fails with a unique violation. Drop the SELECT, rely on the primary key (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING), and retry with a new code when no row is inserted
Add a Redis lock around every insert
qs.e: The primary key already prevents duplicates; the bug is that the app treats the error as a crash. Letting the constraint decide and retrying is simpler and faster than a lock or SERIALIZABLE isolation. Collisions are rare with 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes, so a retry loop is cheap.

interview.q: Design a URL shortener like bit.ly.
answer: Requirements and numbers first: read-heavy (often 100:1), redirect latency target, custom aliases, expiry, analytics.

Code generation trade-off: counter + base62 (no collisions, but codes are guessable and need a shared counter or ID ranges) vs random code + unique constraint + retry (no coordination, rare collisions).
Redirect choice: 301 is cached by browsers (less load, but you lose click counts); 302 keeps every click visible for analytics.
Read path: cache hot codes (Redis), CDN for redirects; write path: one primary database is enough at about 12 writes per second.
Analytics asynchronously through a queue, so a slow analytics store never slows down redirects.
Failure and abuse: cache outage protection, rate limits on creation, malware URL checks.
followups: How do you stop people from guessing private links?
Redis goes down at peak. What happens?
How would you expire links?

interview.q: Design a rate limiter for a public API.
answer: Clarify: limit per API key, user or IP? Strict or approximate? One region or many?
Algorithm trade-off: fixed window (simple, allows 2× bursts at window edges), sliding-window counter (good accuracy, small memory), token bucket (allows controlled bursts, common in gateways).
Where it runs: API gateway or middleware, with shared state in Redis using atomic operations (INCR, or a Lua script for multi-step logic).
Response: HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header so clients back off.
Failure mode: if Redis is down, fail open (allow traffic, risk overload) or fail closed (block traffic, risk outage); say which and why per endpoint.
Multi-region: local limits per region with a slightly lower quota, instead of a slow global counter.
followups: How do you rate-limit a client that rotates IP addresses?
How would you test it?

interview.q: Design a chat app like KakaoTalk or WhatsApp, with 1:1 and group chats.
answer: Requirements: 1:1 and groups, delivery and read receipts, offline delivery, message history, presence; message ordering inside one conversation.
Connections: clients keep a WebSocket to a gateway tier; a lookup of which gateway holds each user routes messages.
Storage: messages partitioned by conversation id, ordered by a time-sortable id; estimate size (tens of TB per year at 10M DAU).
Delivery: store first, then push; clients acknowledge; unacknowledged messages are sent on reconnect or through mobile push notifications.
Groups: fan-out to members at send time for small groups; cap or handle large groups differently.
Failures: gateway crash (clients reconnect and resync from the last seen id), duplicate sends (client-generated message id as idempotency key).
followups: How do you keep message order when a user has two devices?
How does presence (online/offline) work without overloading the system?

videos.t: How to Prepare for System Design Interviews w/ Meta Staff Engineer
videos.why: How to prepare, from a staff-level interviewer.

videos.t: System Design Interview: A Step-By-Step Guide
videos.why: A step-by-step framework for the interview itself.

one: Questions like "tell me about a conflict" or "a project that failed" test how you work. Prepared, specific stories with your actions and results win.
an: Bringing case files instead of opinions: "here is what happened, what I did, and the outcome".
how: Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action (most of the time here, using "I"), Result (numbers if possible), plus what you learned.
Prepare 6–8 stories that each cover several themes: conflict, failure, leadership without authority, tight deadline, ambiguity, mentoring, a hard technical decision.
Be honest about failures and show what changed afterwards.
Ask good questions at the end about the team, on-call, how decisions are made, and how success is measured.
why: At senior level these rounds carry real weight; strong coders get down-levelled or rejected on them.
trade: Over-rehearsed stories sound scripted. Know the beats, not a script.

myth.r: They often decide level and hire/no-hire between technically similar candidates.

q.s: "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate." Strongest answer shape?
o: "I never disagree with people."
A specific situation, how you understood their view, the data or experiment you used, the decision, and the result
A story where you were right and they were wrong
A general philosophy of teamwork
q.e: Specific, collaborative, evidence-driven, with an outcome.

more: Answering "why are you leaving / why us"
Culture and language differences in interviews
lab: Write 6 STAR stories from your real projects in a doc, each under 200 words, tagged with themes. Practise telling two of them out loud in under 2 minutes each.
docs: Amazon: Leadership principles (used in many behavioral rounds)

plain:
Behavioral interviews ask about real situations: a conflict, a failure, a hard decision, a time you led something. Interviewers want specific stories that show how you work, not general opinions.

Prepare 6–8 true stories in advance and tell them with the STAR structure.
bridge: A good STAR answer is like a good bug report or PR description: what was happening, what you were asked to do, what you changed, and the measured result. A vague “I usually...” answer is like a bug report that only says “it is broken”.

walk.title: Answering “Tell me about a disagreement with a teammate”
steps: Situation: “On our booking app, a teammate wanted to add Redis caching to fix slow venue search before launch.”
Task: “I owned search and believed the problem was a missing index, but I wasn't sure.”

Action: “I suggested we measure first. I ran EXPLAIN on the slow query, showed it was a sequential scan, and added the index in a 30-minute experiment. I also wrote down when caching would become necessary.”
Result: “Search went from 1.4s to 40ms without new infrastructure. We agreed to revisit caching at 10× traffic.”
Learning: “Turning disagreements into small experiments works better than debating.”

terms: Prepared stories that cover many question types.
Your actions vs the team's; interviewers want to know your part.
The quality the interviewer is looking for in your answer.
insights: Interviewers write down evidence while you talk. A number or a named decision is easy to write; a general claim leaves an empty note, which counts as “no signal”.
One good story covers several questions: the index-vs-Redis story fits conflict, data-driven decisions and ownership.
Failure stories are strong if you show what changed afterwards.

prod.summary: At large companies each interviewer is assigned signals to check (for example ownership or handling conflict) and writes notes with evidence. Vague answers leave empty notes, which count as “no signal”. Amazon maps every question to its 16 leadership principles; Korean companies such as Toss run separate culture-fit (컬처핏) interviews; many Korean interviews also open with a 1-minute self-introduction (1분 자기소개).
checklist: Have 6–8 true stories, each tagged with 2–3 themes (conflict, failure, ambiguity, deadline, mentoring, a hard technical call).
Each story has a 2-minute version and a deeper layer ready: real numbers, what you tried first, who disagreed.
Say “I” for your actions and “we” for the team, and be clear which is which.
Every story ends with a result (a number if possible) and what you changed afterwards.
Prepare a 1-minute self-introduction in each interview language you may use (Korean and English), focused on what you build, not your life history.
Read the company's values page and map one story to each value before the interview.
Prepare 3 questions for them: on-call, how decisions are made, how success in the first 6 months is measured.
numbers: Amazon lists 16 leadership principles on amazon.jobs, and its behavioral questions are built around them.
A common target: Situation and Task in about 20–30 seconds, most of a 2-minute answer on Action, and a clear Result.
failures: The interviewer keeps asking “but what did you do?”
Your story used only “we”. Re-tell it with your specific actions: what you measured, wrote, proposed or decided.
Feedback says “answers were generic” even though you answered every question.
You described how you usually work instead of one real event. Start with a specific time and place: “In March, on the payments team...”.
Your failure story is a hidden success (“I work too hard”), and the interviewer looks unconvinced.
Pick a real mistake with real impact, own it without blaming others, and show the process change you made afterwards.
A follow-up question about numbers in your story makes you hesitate or change the figures.
Unprepared detail layer, which can look invented. Write down the real numbers for every story before the interview.

code.title: STAR story card (one per story in your bank)
code.src:
Title:     Index vs Redis disagreement
Themes:    conflict, data-driven decision, ownership

S (20s)  Booking app, venue search slow (1.4s) before launch;
          teammate wanted to add Redis.
T (10s)  I owned search; I suspected a missing index.
A (60s)  - Proposed measuring before deciding
          - Ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE: sequential scan on venues
          - Added a composite index in a 30-min experiment
          - Wrote down when caching would become necessary
R (20s)  p95 1.4s -> 40ms, no new infrastructure;
          agreed to revisit caching at 10x traffic.
Learned  Turn disagreements into small experiments.

Deeper layer (if asked)
  - Exact query and index columns
  - What the teammate said and why it was reasonable
  - What I would do if the index had not helped
code.note: The “Deeper layer” section is what saves you from follow-up questions; interviewers probe until the details run out.

qs.s: You tell a strong project story using “we” throughout. The interviewer then asks three times what you personally did. What is the likely problem in their notes?
o: The story was too short
You did not mention the company's values
You should have used the STAR acronym out loud
They cannot record evidence of your individual actions, so the story gives them almost no signal
qs.e: Interviewers grade your behaviour, not the team's. A “we” story without your own actions leaves their notes empty, even if the project was impressive.

qs.s: “Tell me about a time you failed.” Which answer is strongest?
o: “I deployed a migration that locked a table for 4 minutes at peak. I rolled back, wrote the incident report, and added a migration checklist and a lock-timeout setting; we have had no lock outage since.”
“I am a perfectionist, so I sometimes spend too long on details.”
“A teammate's bug broke production, and I had to fix it over the weekend.”
“I have not really failed; I always test carefully.”
qs.e: It is a real mistake you own, with impact, a fix and a lasting change. The “perfectionist” answer is a disguised strength, and the teammate story blames someone else.

qs.s: In a Korean company's 컬처핏 (culture-fit) interview you are asked: “Why do you want to join us?” Best answer?
o: “Your company is famous and stable.”
“I want to learn a lot from your senior engineers.”
Name a specific product or engineering practice of theirs, connect it to something you have built, and say what you would contribute
“The salary and benefits are better than my current job.”
qs.e: A specific link between their work and your experience shows real interest and fit. “I want to learn” is fine to add but, alone, it is about what you take, not what you bring.

qs.s: Read this answer to “Tell me about a time you had a tight deadline.” What is the main weakness?

code.title: transcript.txt
code.src:
Candidate (1:40): So the company was growing fast, we had a
  big client in Busan, the CEO promised a launch before
  Chuseok, the design team was late, the backend was old
  PHP, our PM had just left, and marketing had already
  bought ads...
Candidate (0:20): So we all worked really hard and we made
  it. Everyone was happy.
Interviewer: What did you do, specifically?

o: The story is too short overall
Almost all the time goes to Situation; there are no specific actions by “I”, no trade-off (what was cut or changed), and the result has no measure
It should not mention the CEO
Tight-deadline stories are always weak; a failure story would be better
qs.e: The interviewer's follow-up shows their notes are empty: they cannot record what you did. A strong version spends about 20 seconds on context and most of the time on your decisions, such as cutting scope, re-ordering work or negotiating the date, with a clear result.

qs.s: A candidate answers “Why are you leaving your current job?” like this. Which rewrite is best?

code.title: transcript.txt
code.src:
Candidate: Honestly, my manager is terrible and the codebase
  is a mess. Nobody there cares about quality, so I am
  wasting my time.

o: Keep it; honesty is always valued
“I have no complaints; everything is perfect there.”
“The salary is too low.”
“I have learned a lot shipping features alone at a small startup. I now want to work on larger systems with strong code review, which is why this platform team interests me.”
qs.e: Interviewers hear complaints as a preview of how you will talk about them. A forward-looking answer that links what you want next to this role is honest and useful. “Everything is perfect” is not believable and gives no reason for the move.

qs.s: “Tell me about a time you received critical feedback.” Which answer is strongest?
o: “My lead said I rarely gave feedback in code reviews. I was annoyed, but I agreed it was true.”
“I usually get positive feedback, so I can't remember a specific case.”

“My lead said my PRs were too large to review. I asked for an example, split my next feature into 4 PRs under 300 lines, and review time went from about 3 days to under 1 day. I still use that limit.”
“A senior said my code was bad, but they were wrong, so I ignored it.”
qs.e: It shows you asked to understand, changed a concrete behaviour, measured the effect and kept the habit. The “I was annoyed, but I agreed it was true” answer admits the point but stops before any change, and a change is exactly what the interviewer wants to hear.

qs.s: You have 3 years of experience and never had a “lead” title. The interviewer asks: “Tell me about a time you led something.” Best approach?
o: Say you have not led anything yet because you never had the title
Tell a story of leading without authority: for example, you drove a library migration, wrote the plan, got two teammates to agree, split the work and tracked it to done
Describe how your tech lead led the project and what you learned from watching
Talk about leading a student club, since it is the only formal role you held
qs.e: Leadership signals are about influence, planning and follow-through, not titles. A workplace example of driving work through other people answers the question directly. Describing someone else's leadership gives no evidence about you.

interview.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager or a more senior engineer.
answer: A specific event with real stakes (a design, a deadline, a technical risk), not a general attitude.
Shows you understood their view first and why it was reasonable.
Your action: data, a small experiment or a written comparison, raised in the right place (1:1, design review), not behind their back.
The outcome, including if you lost: you disagreed, then committed and helped it succeed.
What you learned about influencing decisions; about 2 minutes total, most of it on Action.
followups: What would you have done if they still said no?
Looking back, were you right?

interview.q: Tell me about a mistake you made that affected users or production.
answer: A real mistake you own, with clear impact (“checkout errors for 12 minutes, about 300 failed orders”), no blaming others.
Immediate response: how you noticed, how you stopped the damage (rollback, flag off), who you informed.
Root cause beyond “I was careless”: the missing check, test or process that allowed it.
A systemic fix that outlived you: a CI check, a checklist, an alert, a migration lock timeout.
What you do differently now, said calmly.
followups: How did you communicate it to your team or users?
How do you know the fix works?

interview.q: Tell me about a time requirements were unclear and the deadline was fixed.
answer: Short context: what was unclear and why the date could not move.
How you reduced ambiguity: questions to product, a quick prototype, a written list of assumptions.
The trade-off you proposed explicitly: what you cut or deferred, and who agreed.
How you kept people informed of risk during the work, not only at the end.
Result with a number, and the follow-up on the deferred items, so it was not just dropped.
followups: What did you cut, and was that the right call?
What would you do if product refused to cut scope?

what did you do?"} F --> D["Deeper layer:
real numbers, who disagreed"]
diagrams.caption: What to notice: Action gets the most time, and it uses “I”. The interviewer then probes until the details run out, so the deeper layer must be prepared, not invented.

videos.t: Answering behavioral interview questions is shockingly uncomplicated
videos.why: A simple structure for behavioural answers.

one: Deep-dive rounds ask you to walk through something you built. Show the problem, your decisions and trade-offs, what broke, and the measurable outcome.
an: A museum guide for your own work: why each piece is there, what was tried and rejected, and what the visitor should notice.
how: Structure: problem and users → constraints → architecture (one diagram) → 2–3 key decisions with alternatives considered → a hard bug or incident → results and what you would do differently.
Expect follow-ups: "why Postgres?", "what happens at 10× traffic?", "how did you test it?", "what did it cost?". This atlas's concepts are the vocabulary for these answers.
Your portfolio and side projects count, especially if live with real users, monitoring and documented decisions (ADRs).
why: It is the most direct evidence of level. Interviewers trust real decisions more than textbook answers.
trade: Do not inflate team work as solo work; interviewers probe until it shows. Say "we" for the team and "I" for your part.

myth.m: Side projects do not count as experience.
myth.r: A live project with real users, monitoring and documented trade-offs is strong evidence, especially early in a career.

q.s: An interviewer asks why you chose a PaaS over Kubernetes for your project. Best answer?
o: "Kubernetes is too hard."
Constraints (team size, traffic, budget, time), the alternatives considered, what you gave up, and when you would revisit
"Everyone uses it."
"I didn't think about it."
q.e: Show decision-making, not just the decision.

lab: Pick your strongest project. Write a one-page project brief: problem, architecture diagram, 3 decisions with alternatives, one incident, metrics. Then rehearse a 5-minute walkthrough and answer 10 follow-up questions you write for yourself using this atlas's concepts.
docs: Tech Interview Handbook: Resume and projects

plain:
Many interviews include a deep dive into something you built. Tell it like an engineer: the problem, the constraints, the architecture, the key decisions and their alternatives, something that went wrong, and the measurable result.

Expect follow-up questions that test whether you understand your own choices.
bridge: Your live side projects are strong material, especially ones with real users, monitoring, payments or AI features. Use the concepts from this atlas to explain why you built them the way you did.

walk.title: A 5-minute project walkthrough
steps: Problem (30s): “Foreign students in Korea can't easily find reliable legal answers in their language.”
Architecture (1 min): one diagram: Next.js frontend, API, Postgres with pgvector, an LLM, hosted on a VPS behind Caddy.
Decisions (2 min): “RAG instead of fine-tuning, because laws change; hybrid search because legal terms need exact matches; a VPS over serverless because of long streaming responses.”
Incident (1 min): “The server went down for two weeks; I rebuilt it, and now deployment is scripted and backups are tested.”
Result and next (30s): usage numbers, what you would do differently (monitoring from day one).

terms: Detailed discussion of your own project.
What you gained and gave up with a choice.
insights: Decisions with alternatives show seniority more than a long feature list.
Interviewers dig into one decision until the answers become theory; real memories (an incident, a cost surprise) survive that, invented reasons do not.
Prepare “what breaks first at 10× traffic?” and “how did you test it?” for every project you list on your CV.

prod.summary: Project deep-dives are where interviewers test whether you really made the decisions you claim. They pick one choice and ask “why?” three or four times, then ask about scale, testing, cost and failure. Candidates who built and ran something live, with real users and real incidents, have the easiest time because the answers are memories, not theory.
checklist: One architecture diagram you can draw from memory in under 2 minutes.
Three key decisions, each with the alternatives you rejected and why (cost, time, team skill, scale).
One real incident or hard bug: symptom, how you found the cause, the fix, and what you changed so it cannot happen again.
Real numbers: users, requests per day, latency, monthly cost, test count. Do not round up.
An answer for “what breaks first at 10× traffic?” that names a specific component and why.
A clear split between team work (“we”) and your part (“I”).
What you would do differently, said without being defensive.
failures: Asked “why Postgres?”, you answer “it is popular” and the interviewer moves on looking unconvinced.
No decision record. Prepare the real reason: relational data, transactions for payments, a team that knows SQL, and what you would use instead under different constraints.
Asked “what happens at 10× traffic?”, you say “it will scale, it is on the cloud”.
Name the first bottleneck and the evidence: e.g. database connections on one VPS or a third-party API rate limit; then the change you would make first.
The interviewer asks a detail of a part you did not build and you guess; it falls apart under follow-up.
You presented team work as your own. Say who owned it, explain what you know, and bring the discussion back to your part.
Your walkthrough takes 15 minutes and the interviewer never gets to ask questions.
Too much feature listing. Cut to problem, diagram, 3 decisions, 1 incident, results, in 5 minutes.

code.title: One-page project brief to prepare before every interview
code.src:
Project:   Legal Q&A for foreign students (RAG)
Users:     ~N weekly users, 3 languages  (use the real number)

Diagram:   Next.js -> API -> Postgres + pgvector
                       -> LLM provider (streaming)
           one VPS behind Caddy, daily backups

Decisions (chose / rejected / because)
  1. RAG / fine-tuning / laws change; answers must cite sources
  2. Hybrid search / vector only / legal terms need exact match
  3. VPS / serverless / long streaming responses, fixed cost

Incident
  Server down -> cause -> fix -> now: scripted deploy, tested restore

At 10x traffic, first to break
  LLM rate limit + cost, then DB connections -> queue + pooler

Testing:   what is tested, what is not, and why
Cost:      monthly total and the biggest line
Differently: monitoring and alerts from day one
code.note: Fill this with real numbers only. Every line is the answer to a follow-up question you will be asked.

qs.s: Your app runs on one VPS with Postgres and calls an LLM API. The interviewer asks: “What happens at 10× traffic?” Best answer?
o: “It is on the cloud, so it scales automatically.”

“The first limit is probably the LLM provider's rate limit and cost, then Postgres connections. I would check current usage against those limits, add a queue and a connection pooler, and cache repeated answers.”
“I would move to Kubernetes.”
“I would rewrite it as microservices.”
qs.e: It names specific bottlenecks, how to confirm them, and targeted fixes. A platform change without a named bottleneck is a guess.

qs.s: The interviewer asks “How did you test it?” and your side project has almost no automated tests. Best answer?
o: Claim it has good coverage
Say testing is not important for side projects
Change the subject to the architecture
Say honestly that it has few tests, explain how you checked it (manual flows, monitoring), and name the first tests you would add and why (e.g. the payment or retrieval logic)
qs.e: Honesty plus a prioritised plan shows judgement. A claim of coverage will collapse under one follow-up question.

qs.s: In a team project you built the frontend. The interviewer asks why the database schema used a JSON column. Best response?
o: Say a teammate owned the schema, share what you know of the reason and how it affected your frontend work, then offer to go deeper on your part
Invent a reason so you do not look uninformed
Say “I don't know” and stop
Criticise the teammate's choice
qs.e: Clear ownership boundaries build trust. Interviewers probe invented answers until they break, which hurts more than admitting you did not own that part.

qs.s: Read this part of a project deep dive. What is the strongest recovery for the candidate's next answer?

code.title: transcript.txt
code.src:
Interviewer: Why did you put Kafka between the API and the
  worker?
Candidate: Kafka is the industry standard for scalable
  systems, so it was the obvious choice.
Interviewer: How much traffic does the app get?
Candidate: About 200 orders a day.

o: “It is future-proof: if we grow 1,000×, we will not need to change anything.”

“Honestly, 200 orders a day is about one every 7 minutes. A jobs table in Postgres or a simple queue would have been enough. I chose Kafka partly to learn it; for production at this scale I would pick the simpler option and switch when a measured limit appears.”
“All big companies use Kafka, so it is good practice.”
Move the discussion to the frontend, which you know better
qs.e: The interviewer is testing whether decisions follow constraints. Admitting the mismatch, doing the math and stating what you would choose now shows judgement. “Future-proof” repeats the same unjustified reasoning and invites more probing.

qs.s: A candidate lists these results on their project brief. The interviewer will ask “How did you measure it?” Which line survives that question?

code.title: project-brief.txt
code.src:
Results
 (A) Made the app 3x faster.
 (B) p95 search latency 1.4s -> 120ms after adding a
     trigram index (Grafana, 7-day window, ~2k searches/day).
 (C) Used modern best practices throughout.
 (D) Improved user satisfaction significantly.

o: (A), because a multiplier is easy to understand
(D), because user satisfaction matters most
(C), because best practices are always good
(B), because it names the metric, the change, the measurement tool, the time window and the traffic
qs.e: (B) answers the follow-up before it is asked. “3x faster” is tempting, but faster at what, measured how, at what percentile? Without those details it sounds made up, even when it is true.

qs.s: The interviewer asks: “What would you do differently on this project?” Which answer is strongest?
o: “Nothing, I'm happy with every decision.”
“I would use a newer framework, because the one I used is old.”
“I would add monitoring and alerts from day one. Our two-week outage was found by a user, not by us. Now I add an uptime check and an error-rate alert before the first release.”
“I would work with a bigger team.”
qs.e: It names a specific gap, the real cost it caused, and a habit you changed. “Nothing” sounds defensive, and a framework change without a reason is a preference, not a lesson.

qs.s: Your strongest side project is technically solid but has almost no real users. How should you present it?
o: Present it honestly as a learning project, focus on the decisions, trade-offs and one hard bug, and say what you validated (load test, demo with 5 classmates)
Round the user count up to sound more impressive
Do not mention it; only work projects count
Say it has many users but you cannot share numbers
qs.e: Decisions and debugging stories are valuable without users, and an honest frame protects you from follow-ups. Invented or vague user numbers are one question away from collapsing, and that damages trust in every other story you told.

interview.q: Walk me through the most technically challenging project you have worked on.
answer: In about 5 minutes: problem and users, constraints, one diagram, 2–3 key decisions, one incident, results.
Each decision has the alternatives you rejected and the reason (cost, team skill, scale, time).
A clear split between “we” (the team) and “I” (your part).
One incident told as symptom → cause → fix → what changed so it cannot repeat.
Real numbers: users, requests, latency, cost. Stop and invite questions instead of listing every feature.
followups: Why that database?
What was the hardest bug?
What did you personally build?

interview.q: If usage of your project grew 10× next month, what would break first, and how do you know?
answer: Names one specific component, for example the LLM provider's rate limit or Postgres connections on one VPS, not “it scales on the cloud”.
Gives the evidence: current usage vs the known limit (requests per minute, connection count, CPU).
Orders the next bottlenecks (second and third to break).
Proposes the smallest fix for each: connection pooler, queue, cache, higher plan, and the cost of each.
Says how you would confirm before spending money: a load test or a dashboard check.
followups: How would you load-test it?
What would that cost per month?

interview.q: Tell me about a technical decision on that project that you would reverse today.
answer: A real decision with the original reasoning, which was sensible at the time.
What changed or what you learned (new scale, a cost surprise, an incident).
The cost of the decision so far, with a number if possible.
What you would choose now and the migration path, not only “I'd do it differently”.
Without blaming teammates or being defensive.
followups: Why not reverse it now?
How would you avoid the same mistake on the next project?

diagrams.title: How a project deep-dive really goes: the “why” chain
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram

  participant C as Candidate
  C->>I: 5-min walkthrough (problem, diagram, 3 decisions)
  I->>C: Why Postgres?
  C->>I: Real reason + rejected alternative
  I->>C: Why not vector-only search?
  C->>I: Legal terms need exact match
  I->>C: What breaks first at 10x?
  C->>I: LLM rate limit, then DB connections
  I->>C: Which part did you build?
  C->>I: We built X, I owned Y
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the walkthrough is short; most of the round is follow-ups. Each “why” goes one level deeper, so every decision needs the alternative you rejected and a real reason.
