videos.t: #AskRaghav | How to explain your project in an interview | 5 Points |
videos.why: Five points for explaining a project in an interview.

one: Some companies give a small project or a live pairing session. They grade judgement: scope, structure, tests, communication, and a clear README.
an: A cooking trial shift: they watch how you organise the station and talk to the team, not only the plate.
how: Clarify scope and time budget first; deliver a complete thin slice over a half-finished big one.
Include: README (setup, decisions, trade-offs, what you would do next), tests on core logic, sensible structure, error handling, and a few commits telling the story.
In pairing: think aloud, ask questions, write tests early, and treat the interviewer as a teammate.
why: Common at product companies and startups, including in Korea, where it is often called a 과제 전형 (assignment stage) and usually followed by a review interview about your code. It shows how you work on realistic code, which algorithm tests do not.
trade: Over-building (Kubernetes manifests for a todo app) signals poor judgement. Spend extra time on the README instead.

myth.m: More features means a better take-home.
myth.r: A small, clean, tested, documented solution with explicit trade-offs usually scores higher.

q.s: You have 4 hours for a take-home. Halfway through you realise one requirement is ambiguous. Best move?
o: Guess silently
Make a reasonable assumption, document it in the README, and (if possible) ask the recruiter
Stop working
Implement both versions fully
q.e: Handling ambiguity explicitly is exactly what is being graded.

lab: Do a 3-hour self-set take-home (e.g. a small booking API + UI). Write the README as if for a reviewer. Ask a friend to review it cold and note what confused them.
docs: Tech Interview Handbook: Coding interview prep

plain: Some companies give you a small project to build at home, or a live pairing session. They are evaluating judgement: did you scope it sensibly, structure it cleanly, test the important parts, and explain your decisions?
bridge: Treat it like a small real PR to a team you respect: clear README, sensible commits, tests on the core logic, and honesty about what you skipped.

walk.title: A 4-hour take-home done well
steps: Read the brief twice; list requirements and questions. Email any truly blocking question; otherwise note assumptions.
Build the thinnest complete version first: the main flow working end to end.
Add tests on the core logic and handle the obvious errors.
Stop on time. Write the README: how to run, decisions and trade-offs, assumptions, what you would do with more time.
In the review call, explain one decision and one thing you would change. Reviewers value that more than extra features.

terms: An assignment done on your own time.
Solving a problem live together with an interviewer.
The document explaining how to run and understand the project.
insights: The README is read first, and it is the only place your reasoning is visible when you are not in the room.
Commit history is read as a story; one giant “initial commit” hides how you work.
In the review call, pointing out your own weak spot before the reviewer does reads as seniority, not weakness.

prod.summary: A reviewer usually reads your README first, runs your project with the commands you gave, reads the core logic and tests, then looks at commit history. In the follow-up interview they ask why you made each choice and what you would change. A project that does not start on their machine often ends the review early.
checklist: Run your setup from a fresh clone, exactly as the README says. If it fails for you, it fails for them.
Pin versions (lockfile committed, Node version stated) and give one command to start and one to test.
Tests cover the core business logic and at least one error path, not only the happy path.
README lists assumptions, trade-offs, what you skipped on purpose, and what you would do next.
Commits are small and readable: they tell the story of how you built it.
No secrets in the repository; use an .env.example.
Check the company's rules on time limits and AI tools, follow them, and say in the README what you used.
failures: The reviewer writes “could not run the project”.
Missing env variable, unpinned dependency, or a step that only works on your machine. Fix: test from a clean clone, commit the lockfile, provide .env.example and defaults.
Feedback: “over-engineered for the scope”.
Microservices, Docker Compose with five services, or a custom framework for a small CRUD task. Use the simplest structure and explain in the README how it would grow.
Feedback: “no evidence of testing” even though the app works.
Tests are missing or only snapshot the UI. Add focused tests for the core logic and one failure case.
In the review call you cannot explain a part of your own code.
Copied code or AI output you did not understand. Only submit code you can explain line by line.

code.title: Take-home README skeleton reviewers can scan in 2 minutes
code.src:
# Booking API (take-home)

## Run
  Node 22, pnpm 9
  cp .env.example .env
  pnpm install && pnpm dev        # http://localhost:3000
  pnpm test

## What works
  - Create / list / cancel bookings
  - Double-booking prevented (DB unique constraint + 409)

## Assumptions
  - One timezone (Asia/Seoul); the brief did not say
  - Auth is out of scope

## Trade-offs
  - SQLite instead of Postgres: zero setup for reviewers;
    the queries are standard SQL and would port as-is
  - No caching: not needed at this scale

## Skipped on purpose / next steps
  - Pagination, rate limiting, e2e tests

## Time spent: ~4h.  AI tools: (state what you used, per the rules)
code.note: The Assumptions and Trade-offs sections are what reviewers grade most; they show judgement that code alone cannot show.

qs.s: You have a 4-hour take-home. At 3h30 the main flow works, but there are no tests and no README. What do you do with the last 30 minutes?
o: Add one more feature to stand out
Refactor the folder structure
Write tests for the core logic and a README with setup, assumptions and trade-offs; list the extra feature under next steps
Ask for more time
qs.e: Reviewers grade judgement and finish. A working core with tests and a clear README beats an extra untested feature.

qs.s: Which README line gives the reviewer the most useful signal?
o: “This project uses React and Node.”
“I used SQLite instead of Postgres so reviewers need no setup; queries are standard SQL, so moving to Postgres is a config change.”
“Built with best practices.”
“Thanks for the opportunity!”
qs.e: It states a decision, the reason, and the cost of changing it later. The other lines carry no information about your thinking.

qs.s: A take-home brief says nothing about AI coding tools. What is the most professional move?
o: Use them freely and say nothing
Never use them, and do not mention it
Use them only for tests
Ask the recruiter about the policy; if you use them, say how in the README, and make sure you can explain every line in the review call
qs.e: Policies differ by company. Asking and disclosing protects you, and the review call will test whether you understand the code anyway.

qs.s: A reviewer reads this handler from your take-home and sends two identical requests at the same moment. What happens, and what is the best fix?

code.title: bookings.ts

o: Both requests can pass the check and create two bookings; add a unique constraint on (roomId, date) and turn the unique-violation error (Prisma P2002) into a 409
Nothing; await makes the requests run one after another
Add a 100 ms delay before create so the first request finishes
Cache existing bookings in memory and check the cache instead
qs.e: Node interleaves requests at every await, so both findFirst calls can see no row. Only the database can enforce uniqueness across concurrent requests. A delay or an in-memory cache only makes the race rarer, and the cache breaks with more than one server process.

qs.s: The brief says: “Stays of more than 7 nights get 10% off. Nights must be 1 to 30.” These are your only tests. Which test adds the most value next?

code.title: pricing.test.ts

o: A snapshot test of the whole result object
A test for 5 nights
Boundary tests: 7 nights has no discount, 8 nights has 10% off, and 0 or 31 nights is rejected
A test that priceFor is a function
qs.e: Bugs live at the edges of rules: “more than 7” versus “7 or more” is the classic off-by-one, and invalid input is the error path reviewers look for. Another happy-path value like 5 nights tests the same branch again.

qs.s: In a live pairing round, the interviewer suggests an approach you think is worse than yours. Best move?
o: Agree silently, because the interviewer is always right
Refuse and continue with your approach
Ask the interviewer to decide everything so you avoid mistakes
Say briefly why you prefer your approach (one trade-off), ask what they see in theirs, then agree on one and continue; if they insist, try theirs and note the risk
qs.e: Pairing rounds grade how you work with a teammate: stating a trade-off and then committing is the signal. Silent agreement hides your judgement, and refusing shows you are hard to work with. Sometimes the suggestion is a hint toward a simpler solution.

qs.s: A take-home says “please spend about 4 hours”. You could easily spend 15 hours and add many features. What is the best choice?
o: Spend 15 hours; more polish always scores higher
Stay close to 4 hours, state the real time spent in the README, and list what you would add next
Spend 2 hours to show you are fast
Spend 15 hours but write “4 hours” in the README
qs.e: The time budget is part of the test: reviewers compare scope decisions made under the same limit. Big over-delivery can read as poor prioritisation, and misreporting time is dishonest, which is worse than any missing feature.

interview.q: (Review call) Walk me through your submission. What would you change before this went to production?
answer: A 2-minute tour: structure, the core logic, where the tests are, the main assumption.
A specific production list ordered by risk: authentication, input validation, concurrency (unique constraints), logging and metrics, migrations, rate limits.
Says which of these you skipped on purpose and why the time went elsewhere.
Points to one weak spot in your own code before the reviewer finds it.
Calm, not defensive: treats the review like a normal PR review.
followups: Which of those would you do first, and why?
How would you deploy this?

interview.q: (Review call) Why did you structure the code this way? For example, why no ORM, or why this folder layout?
answer: The actual reason tied to the brief: size of the task, reviewer setup time, testability.
The alternative you considered and what it would have cost.
When your choice stops being right (more entities, more developers, a second service).
No invented reasoning after the fact; if it was a default, say so and evaluate it now.
followups: What would you change if three more developers joined?
How would you test the database layer?

interview.q: (Live extension) Add a new rule to your code now: cancellations within 24 hours of the booking are not refunded.
answer: Clarify first: 24 hours before the stay starts, or after booking? Which timezone?
Find where the rule belongs (domain logic, not the HTTP handler) and explain that choice.
Write a failing test first for the edge (exactly 24 hours), then the code.
Mention the side effects: existing bookings, the API response, the README.
Think aloud and keep the change small; finishing a tested slice beats a half-done big change.
followups: How would you make the 24-hour window configurable?
How do you test time-dependent code without waiting?
